regulation_query: lawful bases for processing personal data, legal grounds for data processing, GDPR
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-6-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-6-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-6-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-6-4-2016-05-04
answer: Under the GDPR, processing of personal data is lawful only if at least one of the following applies: (a) the data subject has given consent for one or more specific purposes; (b) processing is necessary for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is party or to take steps at the request of the data subject prior to entering into a contract; (c) processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject; (d) processing is necessary to protect the vital interests of the data subject or another natural person; (e) processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller; (f) processing is necessary for the purposes of the legitimate interests pursued by the controller or a third party, except where overridden by the interests or fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject, particularly if the data subject is a child. Public authorities do not rely on point (f) for processing in the performance of their tasks. The legal basis for processing under points (c) and (e) must be laid down by Union or Member State law, which must meet an objective of public interest and be proportionate to the legitimate aim pursued [2].

regulation_query: personal data breach notification obligations, supervisory authority, GDPR
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-33-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-33-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-33-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-33-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-33-5-2016-05-04
answer: A personal data breach must be notified to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after the controller becomes aware of it, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. If the notification is not made within 72 hours, it must be accompanied by reasons for the delay [1].

regulation_query: Meldepflicht bei Datenschutzverletzungen, Benachrichtigung der betroffenen Personen, Datenschutz-Grundverordnung (DSGVO)
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-de-article-34-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-de-article-34-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-de-article-34-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-de-article-34-4-2016-05-04
answer: Eine Verletzung des Schutzes personenbezogener Daten muss den betroffenen Personen unverzüglich mitgeteilt werden, wenn sie voraussichtlich ein hohes Risiko für die persönlichen Rechte und Freiheiten natürlicher Personen zur Folge hat. Die Benachrichtigung muss in klarer und einfacher Sprache die Art der Verletzung beschreiben und mindestens die in Art. 33 Abs. 3 Buchstaben b, c und d genannten Informationen und Maßnahmen enthalten. Eine Benachrichtigung ist nicht erforderlich, wenn der Verantwortliche geeignete technische und organisatorische Sicherheitsvorkehrungen getroffen hat, durch nachfolgende Maßnahmen das hohe Risiko aller Wahrscheinlichkeit nach nicht mehr besteht oder die Benachrichtigung mit unverhältnismäßigem Aufwand verbunden wäre. In diesem letzten Fall ist stattdessen eine öffentliche Bekanntmachung oder eine ähnliche Maßnahme vorzunehmen, durch die die betroffenen Personen vergleichbar wirksam informiert werden [1].

regulation_query: designation of data protection officer, data protection officer obligations, GDPR
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-37-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-37-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-37-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-37-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-37-5-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-37-6-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-37-7-2016-05-04
answer: A company is required to designate a data protection officer if: (a) the processing is carried out by a public authority or body, except for courts acting in their judicial capacity; (b) the core activities of the company consist of processing operations which, by their nature, scope and/or purposes, require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale; or (c) the core activities consist of processing on a large scale of special categories of data pursuant to Article 9 or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences referred to in Article 10 [1].

regulation_query: maximum administrative fine, penalties, GDPR
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-83-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-83-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-83-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-83-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-83-5-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-83-6-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-83-7-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-83-9-2016-05-04
answer: Under the GDPR, the maximum administrative fine depends on the nature of the infringement. For infringements of the obligations of the controller and processor pursuant to Articles 8, 11, 25 to 39 and 42 and 43, the fine can be up to 10,000,000 EUR or, in the case of an undertaking, up to 2% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher. For infringements of the basic principles for processing, data subjects' rights, transfers of personal data to third countries, and other specified obligations, the fine can be up to 20,000,000 EUR or, in the case of an undertaking, up to 4% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [1].

regulation_query: data protection impact assessment, mandatory conditions, GDPR
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-35-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-5-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-6-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-7-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-8-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-9-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-10-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-35-11-2016-05-04
answer: A data protection impact assessment (DPIA) is mandatory prior to processing when a type of processing, particularly using new technologies and considering the nature, scope, context, and purposes, is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. Specifically, a DPIA is required in cases of: (a) systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing including profiling, leading to decisions with legal or similarly significant effects on the person; (b) large-scale processing of special categories of data or data relating to criminal convictions and offences; and (c) systematic large-scale monitoring of publicly accessible areas. The DPIA must be carried out before the processing begins and include a systematic description of the processing, assessment of necessity and proportionality, risk assessment, and measures to address risks. The controller must seek advice from the data protection officer if designated and may seek views of data subjects where appropriate. Exceptions apply if the processing is based on Union or Member State law that already includes a DPIA as part of a general impact assessment, unless Member States require otherwise. Additionally, the DPIA must be reviewed when there is a change in the risk posed by the processing operations [1].

regulation_query: obligation to maintain records of processing activities, data controller, data processor, exemption for organizations with fewer than 250 employees, GDPR
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-30-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-30-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-30-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-30-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-30-5-2016-05-04
answer: According to GDPR Art. 30(5), the obligation to maintain records of processing activities does not apply to an enterprise or organisation employing fewer than 250 persons unless one of the following conditions is met: the processing is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects, the processing is not occasional, or the processing includes special categories of data as referred to in Article 9(1) or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences referred to in Article 10 [1].

regulation_query: automated individual decision-making, solely algorithmic decision, right to object, data subject rights, GDPR
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-22-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-22-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-22-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-22-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-21-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-21-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-21-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-21-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-21-5-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-21-6-2016-05-04 aia-en-article-86-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-86-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-86-3-2026-07-27
answer: Yes, under GDPR Art. 22(1), a data subject has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning them or similarly significantly affects them. However, this right does not apply if the decision is necessary for entering into or performance of a contract, is authorized by Union or Member State law with suitable safeguards, or is based on the data subject's explicit consent. In such cases, the controller must implement suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights, including the right to obtain human intervention, to express their point of view, and to contest the decision [2]. Additionally, under GDPR Art. 21(1), the data subject can object to processing based on certain legal grounds, which may include automated decision-making, unless the controller demonstrates compelling legitimate grounds overriding the data subject's interests [1]. Furthermore, the AI Act Art. 86 provides that affected persons subject to decisions based on high-risk AI systems have the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations of the AI's role in the decision-making [3].

regulation_query: contractual obligations between data controller and data processor, GDPR requirements for data processing agreements, roles and responsibilities of controller and processor
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-28-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-28-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-28-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-28-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-28-5-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-28-6-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-28-7-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-28-8-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-28-9-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-28-10-2016-05-04
answer: A contract between a controller and a processor must be a binding legal act that sets out the subject-matter and duration of the processing, the nature and purpose of the processing, the type of personal data and categories of data subjects, and the obligations and rights of the controller. It must stipulate that the processor: (a) processes personal data only on documented instructions from the controller, including regarding transfers to third countries or international organisations, unless required by law; (b) ensures confidentiality of persons authorised to process the data; (c) takes all measures required pursuant to Article 32; (d) respects conditions for engaging another processor; (e) assists the controller in responding to data subject rights requests; (f) assists the controller in compliance with Articles 32 to 36; (g) deletes or returns all personal data after the end of the service provision, unless law requires storage; and (h) makes available to the controller all information necessary to demonstrate compliance and allows audits. The processor must inform the controller if an instruction infringes the Regulation. The contract must be in writing, including electronic form [1].

regulation_query: transfer of personal data to third countries, conditions for international data transfer, GDPR
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-44-0-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-45-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-46-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-46-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-49-1-2016-05-04
answer: Personal data may be transferred to a country outside the EU only if the conditions laid down in Chapter V of the GDPR are complied with by the controller and processor, ensuring that the level of protection of natural persons guaranteed by the GDPR is not undermined [2]. Specifically, transfers may take place if: 1) the Commission has decided that the third country or international organisation ensures an adequate level of protection, in which case no specific authorisation is required [9]; 2) in the absence of an adequacy decision, the controller or processor provides appropriate safeguards, such as contractual clauses or administrative arrangements, with enforceable data subject rights and effective legal remedies [6][8]; or 3) if neither adequacy decisions nor appropriate safeguards are in place, transfers may occur only under specific derogations for particular situations, such as explicit consent of the data subject after being informed of risks, necessity for contract performance, important public interest reasons, legal claims, protection of vital interests, or transfers from public registers, among others [4]. The controller must assess all circumstances and provide suitable safeguards if relying on compelling legitimate interests for transfers not covered by other provisions [4].

regulation_query: Recht auf Löschung, Ausnahmen, Datenschutz-Grundverordnung, GDPR
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-de-article-17-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-de-article-17-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-de-article-17-3-2016-05-04
answer: Vom Recht auf Löschung gemäß Art. 17 Abs. 1 GDPR gibt es Ausnahmen, wenn die Verarbeitung der personenbezogenen Daten erforderlich ist: a) zur Ausübung des Rechts auf freie Meinungsäußerung und Information; b) zur Erfüllung einer rechtlichen Verpflichtung, die die Verarbeitung nach dem Recht der Union oder der Mitgliedstaaten erfordert, oder zur Wahrnehmung einer Aufgabe, die im öffentlichen Interesse liegt oder in Ausübung öffentlicher Gewalt erfolgt, die dem Verantwortlichen übertragen wurde; c) aus Gründen des öffentlichen Interesses im Bereich der öffentlichen Gesundheit gemäß Art. 9 Abs. 2 Buchstaben h und i sowie Art. 9 Abs. 3; d) für im öffentlichen Interesse liegende Archivzwecke, wissenschaftliche oder historische Forschungszwecke oder für statistische Zwecke gemäß Art. 89 Abs. 1, soweit das Recht auf Löschung voraussichtlich die Verwirklichung der Ziele dieser Verarbeitung unmöglich macht oder ernsthaft beeinträchtigt; oder e) zur Geltendmachung, Ausübung oder Verteidigung von Rechtsansprüchen [1].

regulation_query: verbotene KI-Praktiken, AI Act, KI-Verordnung
cited_chunk_ids: aia-de-article-5-1-2026-07-27 aia-de-article-5-1-2026-07-27-p3 aia-de-article-5-1a-2026-07-27 aia-de-article-5-1b-2026-07-27 aia-de-article-5-4-2026-07-27 aia-de-article-5-7-2026-07-27 aia-de-article-5-8-2026-07-27 omnibus_ai-de-article-1-0-2026-07-24-p3 omnibus_ai-de-article-1-0-2026-07-24-p4 omnibus_ai-de-article-1-0-2026-07-24-p5
answer:
Nach der KI-Verordnung sind folgende Praktiken im KI-Bereich verboten: a) das Inverkehrbringen, die Inbetriebnahme oder die Verwendung eines KI-Systems, das Techniken der unterschwelligen Beeinflussung außerhalb des Bewusstseins einer Person oder absichtlich manipulative oder täuschende Techniken einsetzt, um das Verhalten einer Person wesentlich zu verändern und sie zu einer Entscheidung zu veranlassen, die sie sonst nicht getroffen hätte, wobei dieser Person oder anderen erheblicher Schaden droht; b) das Inverkehrbringen, die Inbetriebnahme oder die Verwendung eines KI-Systems, das die Vulnerabilität bestimmter Personen ausnutzt, um ihr Verhalten wesentlich zu verändern und erheblichen Schaden zu verursachen; ba) das Inverkehrbringen, die Inbetriebnahme oder die Verwendung eines KI-Systems, das realistische Bild-, Video-, Ton- oder ähnliche Inhalte erzeugt oder manipuliert, in denen intime Körperteile oder an eindeutig sexuellen Handlungen beteiligte Personen dargestellt werden, ohne deren ausdrückliche Zustimmung; bb) das Inverkehrbringen, die Inbetriebnahme oder die Verwendung eines KI-Systems, das Material im Sinne der Richtlinie 2011/93/EU erzeugt oder manipuliert, es sei denn, das Verhalten ist nach nationalem Recht gerechtfertigt; c) die Verwendung von KI-Systemen zur sozialen Bewertung von Personen, die zu ungerechtfertigter oder unverhältnismäßiger Schlechterstellung führt; d) das Inverkehrbringen, die Inbetriebnahme oder Verwendung von KI-Systemen, die eine konkrete Gefahr für Leben oder körperliche Unversehrtheit darstellen oder zur Terrorismusbekämpfung eingesetzt werden; iii) das Aufspüren oder Identifizieren von Personen zu Strafverfolgungszwecken für bestimmte schwere Straftaten [1].

Diese Verbote gelten unter Berücksichtigung der in der Verordnung genannten Ausnahmen und Bedingungen, insbesondere bei der Erzeugung oder Manipulation von Inhalten, die nur verboten ist, wenn sie Zweck des KI-Systems ist oder ein vorhersehbares Ergebnis ohne angemessene Schutzmaßnahmen darstellt [1][3].

regulation_query: AI system used as safety component in the management and operation of critical infrastructure, supply of electricity, high-risk classification, AI Act
cited_chunk_ids: aia-en-annex-iii-0-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-1a-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-1b-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-1c-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-3-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-4-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-5-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-6-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-7-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-8-2026-07-27
answer: Yes, an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, including electricity supply, is considered high-risk according to Annex III of the AI Act [4]. Furthermore, Article 6(1) states that an AI system is high-risk if it is intended as a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation and requires third-party conformity assessment, which would apply to critical infrastructure such as the electricity grid [1].

regulation_query: high-risk AI systems, stand-alone AI systems, Annex III AI Act, date of application, obligations
cited_chunk_ids: aia-en-article-6-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-1a-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-1b-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-1c-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-3-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-4-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-5-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-6-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-7-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-6-8-2026-07-27
answer: The high-risk obligations for stand-alone AI systems referred to in Annex III apply from the time the system is placed on the market or put into service. Providers must document their assessment if they consider such a system is not high-risk before placing it on the market or putting it into service, and they are subject to registration obligations. The Commission will provide guidelines specifying the practical implementation of these rules by 2 February 2026, which may clarify the timing and conditions further [1].

regulation_query: transparency obligations, customer-service chatbot, AI system, AI Act
cited_chunk_ids: aia-en-article-50-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-3-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-4-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-5-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-6-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-7-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-13-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-13-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-13-3-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-16-0-2026-07-27
answer: A customer-service chatbot, as an AI system intended to interact directly with natural persons, must be designed and developed so that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the perspective of a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect natural person, considering the circumstances and context of use [1](1). Additionally, if the chatbot generates synthetic audio, image, video or text content, the outputs must be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, unless the system performs only an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data or semantics, or is authorized by law for criminal offence purposes [1](2). The information about the AI nature of the system must be provided clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure, conforming to applicable accessibility requirements [1](5). If the chatbot qualifies as a high-risk AI system, it must be designed and developed to ensure sufficient transparency to enable deployers to interpret its output and use it appropriately, and be accompanied by instructions for use containing detailed information such as provider identity, system capabilities, limitations, accuracy metrics, and human oversight measures [2]. Providers of high-risk AI systems have further obligations including ensuring compliance with requirements, providing documentation, and affixing CE marking [3].

regulation_query: obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems, AI Act
answer: Deployers of high-risk AI systems have several obligations: (1) They must take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure use in accordance with the instructions for use [1](1). (2) They must assign human oversight to competent, trained, and authorized natural persons with necessary support [1](2). (3) They must ensure input data is relevant and sufficiently representative if they control the input data [1](4). (4) They must monitor the operation of the system per instructions, inform providers and authorities without undue delay if risks or serious incidents arise, and suspend use if necessary [1](5). (5) They must keep logs for at least six months unless otherwise provided by law [1](6). (6) Employers deploying such systems at workplaces must inform workers and their representatives before use [1](7). (7) Public authorities and EU institutions deploying such systems must comply with registration obligations and not use unregistered systems [1](8). (8) They must use information provided under Article 13 to comply with data protection impact assessment obligations under GDPR or Directive (EU) 2016/680 [1](9). (9) For post-remote biometric identification, deployers must request judicial authorization and report to authorities, with certain exclusions and possible stricter national laws [1](10). (10) Deployers making decisions related to natural persons must inform those persons about the use of the high-risk AI system [1](11). (11) They must cooperate with competent authorities in actions related to the AI system [1](12).

regulation_query: fundamental rights impact assessment, obligation, responsible party, GDPR, AI Act
cited_chunk_ids: aia-en-article-27-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-27-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-27-3-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-27-4-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-27-5-2026-07-27
answer: A fundamental rights impact assessment must be carried out by deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2), except for those intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III. Specifically, this applies to deployers that are bodies governed by public law, private entities providing public services, and deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in points 5 (b) and (c) of Annex III. This assessment is required prior to deploying the high-risk AI system for the first time, and must be updated if any relevant elements change during use [1].

regulation_query: AI literacy obligation, AI Act, requirements for users and deployers of AI systems
cited_chunk_ids: aia-en-article-4-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-4-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-4-3-2026-07-27 omnibus_ai-en-article-1-0-2026-07-24-p2
answer: The AI literacy obligation requires providers and deployers of AI systems to take measures to support the development of AI literacy among their staff and other persons involved in the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf. This support must consider the technical knowledge, experience, education, training, and the context in which the AI systems are used, as well as the persons or groups on whom the AI systems are used. However, this obligation does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy of any individual. Additionally, the Commission and Member States shall support and facilitate these efforts, especially for SMEs, including by publishing practical examples on a single information platform. The Board shall adopt recommendations to support the promotion of AI literacy, taking into account European competence frameworks and setting common objectives [1][4].

regulation_query: general-purpose AI system, systemic risk, high-risk classification, obligations, AI Act
cited_chunk_ids: aia-en-article-51-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-51-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-51-3-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-55-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-55-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-55-3-2026-07-27
answer: A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have systemic risk if the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating point operations, is greater than 10^25 [1](2). When a general-purpose AI model is classified as having systemic risk, its providers have additional obligations beyond those for general-purpose AI models. These include performing model evaluation using standardized protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks; assessing and mitigating possible systemic risks at the Union level; promptly reporting serious incidents and corrective measures to the AI Office and national authorities; and ensuring adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure [2](1). Providers may rely on approved codes of practice or European harmonised standards to demonstrate compliance, or otherwise must demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance [2](2). All information obtained under these obligations, including trade secrets, must be treated confidentially [2](3).

regulation_query: prohibited AI practices, penalties, sanctions, AI Act
cited_chunk_ids: aia-en-article-99-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-99-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-99-3-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-99-4-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-99-5-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-99-6-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-99-6a-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-99-7-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-99-8-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-99-9-2026-07-27
answer: Non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices referred to in Article 5 of the AI Act shall be subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 35,000,000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7% of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [3].

regulation_query: entities subject to DORA, scope of DORA, financial entities, ICT risk management, digital operational resilience
cited_chunk_ids: dora-en-article-2-1-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-2-2-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-2-3-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-2-4-2022-12-27
answer: DORA applies to a range of financial entities including credit institutions, payment institutions (including exempted ones), account information service providers, electronic money institutions (including exempted ones), investment firms, crypto-asset service providers and issuers of asset-referenced tokens, central securities depositories, central counterparties, trading venues, trade repositories, managers of alternative investment funds, management companies, data reporting service providers, insurance and reinsurance undertakings, insurance intermediaries, reinsurance intermediaries and ancillary insurance intermediaries, institutions for occupational retirement provision, credit rating agencies, administrators of critical benchmarks, crowdfunding service providers, securitisation repositories, and ICT third-party service providers [1]. However, certain entities are excluded from the scope, such as managers of alternative investment funds as per Directive 2011/61/EU, insurance and reinsurance undertakings as per Directive 2009/138/EC, institutions for occupational retirement provision with 15 or fewer members, certain exempted natural or legal persons under Directive 2014/65/EU, micro, small or medium-sized insurance intermediaries, reinsurance intermediaries and ancillary insurance intermediaries, and post office giro institutions as per Directive 2013/36/EU [1]. Member States may also exclude certain entities listed in Directive 2013/36/EU from the scope within their territories, with notification to the Commission [1]. Collectively, the entities listed in points (a) to (t) of paragraph 1 are referred to as 'financial entities' under DORA [1].

regulation_query: ICT risk management responsibility, financial entity, DORA, ultimate responsibility, management body
cited_chunk_ids: dora-en-article-5-1-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-5-2-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-5-3-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-5-4-2022-12-27
answer: The management body of the financial entity bears the ultimate responsibility for managing the financial entity’s ICT risk. They are responsible for defining, approving, overseeing, and implementing all arrangements related to the ICT risk management framework, including setting policies, roles, responsibilities, governance arrangements, and approving the digital operational resilience strategy and related plans [2].

regulation_query: ICT risk management framework, review frequency, DORA
cited_chunk_ids: dora-en-article-6-1-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-6-2-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-6-3-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-6-4-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-6-5-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-6-6-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-6-7-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-6-8-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-6-9-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-6-10-2022-12-27
answer: The ICT risk management framework must be reviewed at least once a year, or periodically in the case of microenterprises, as well as upon the occurrence of major ICT-related incidents, and following supervisory instructions or conclusions derived from relevant digital operational resilience testing or audit processes [2].

regulation_query: major ICT-related incident reporting obligations, deadlines for incident reports, DORA
cited_chunk_ids: dora-en-article-19-1-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-3-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-4-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-5-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-6-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-8-2022-12-27
answer: For a major ICT-related incident, financial entities must submit the following reports to the relevant competent authority within the time limits to be laid down in accordance with Article 20: (a) an initial notification; (b) an intermediate report after the initial notification as soon as the status of the original incident has changed significantly or the handling of the incident has changed based on new information, followed by updated notifications whenever a relevant status update is available or upon specific request of the competent authority; (c) a final report when the root cause analysis has been completed and actual impact figures are available to replace estimates. The initial notification and reports must include all information necessary for the competent authority to determine the significance of the incident and assess possible cross-border impacts. If technical impossibility prevents submission of the initial notification using the template, alternative means must be used. Financial entities may outsource reporting obligations but remain fully responsible for compliance [2]. The exact deadlines for submission are to be specified in Article 20, which is not provided here [2(4)].

answer: Ein bedrohungsorientierter Penetrationstest (TLPT) muss mindestens alle drei Jahre durchgeführt werden. Die zuständige Behörde kann jedoch auf Grundlage des Risikoprofils des Finanzunternehmens und unter Berücksichtigung der betrieblichen Gegebenheiten die Häufigkeit dieser Tests verringern oder erhöhen [1].

regulation_query: register of information on ICT third-party arrangements, ICT third-party risk management, DORA
cited_chunk_ids: dora-en-article-28-3-2022-12-27
answer: The register of information on ICT third-party arrangements is a documented record that financial entities must maintain and update at entity level, as well as at sub-consolidated and consolidated levels, as part of their ICT risk management framework. This register includes all contractual arrangements concerning the use of ICT services provided by ICT third-party service providers. It must distinguish between arrangements that cover ICT services supporting critical or important functions and those that do not. Financial entities are required to report at least yearly to competent authorities on the number of new arrangements, the categories of ICT third-party service providers, the types of contractual arrangements, and the ICT services and functions provided. Upon request, the full register or specified sections must be made available to competent authorities to enable effective supervision. Additionally, financial entities must inform competent authorities in a timely manner about any planned contractual arrangements on ICT services supporting critical or important functions, as well as when a function becomes critical or important [4].

regulation_query: ICT outsourcing contract, critical functions, contractual provisions, DORA, operational resilience, third-party risk management
cited_chunk_ids: dora-en-article-30-1-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-30-2-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-30-3-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-30-3-2022-12-27-p2
answer:
An ICT outsourcing contract supporting critical functions must include the elements listed in DORA Art. 30(2) plus additional specific provisions in Art. 30(3). These include:

- A clear and complete description of all functions and ICT services provided, including subcontracting conditions (Art. 30(2)(a)).
- Locations where services and data processing occur, with notification requirements for changes (Art. 30(2)(b)).
- Provisions on data protection including availability, authenticity, integrity, and confidentiality (Art. 30(2)(c)).
- Provisions ensuring access, recovery, and return of data in case of insolvency or contract termination (Art. 30(2)(d)).
- Service level descriptions with updates (Art. 30(2)(e)).
- Obligations for assistance during ICT incidents at no or pre-agreed cost (Art. 30(2)(f)).
- Cooperation obligations with competent and resolution authorities (Art. 30(2)(g)).
- Termination rights and minimum notice periods (Art. 30(2)(h)).
- Conditions for participation in ICT security awareness and resilience training (Art. 30(2)(i)).

Additionally, for critical or important functions, contracts must include:

- Full service level descriptions with precise quantitative and qualitative performance targets for effective monitoring and corrective actions (Art. 30(3)(a)).
- Notice periods and reporting obligations for events impacting service provision (Art. 30(3)(b)).
- Requirements for business contingency plans and ICT security measures (Art. 30(3)(c)).
- Obligation to participate and cooperate in threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) (Art. 30(3)(d)).
- Rights to ongoing monitoring, including unrestricted access, inspection, audit rights, cooperation during audits, and details on audit scope and frequency (Art. 30(3)(e)).
- Exit strategies with mandatory transition periods to reduce disruption risk (Art. 30(3)(f)).

These provisions ensure comprehensive contractual coverage for ICT services supporting critical functions in financial entities [1].

regulation_query: ransomware attack, personal data breach, customer data exposure, reporting obligations, data breach notification, GDPR, DORA, financial sector, incident reporting, supervisory authority, affected data subjects
cited_chunk_ids: gdpr-en-article-34-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-34-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-34-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-34-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-33-1-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-33-2-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-33-3-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-33-4-2016-05-04 gdpr-en-article-33-5-2016-05-04 dora-en-article-19-1-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-2-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-4-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-5-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-6-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-7-2022-12-27
answer:
Under the GDPR, if the ransomware attack results in a personal data breach likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the bank (as the data controller) must notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it, unless the breach is unlikely to result in such risk. The notification must describe the nature of the breach, including categories and approximate number of data subjects and records concerned, contact details of the data protection officer, likely consequences, and measures taken or proposed to address the breach. If the breach is likely to result in a high risk, the bank must also communicate the breach to the affected data subjects without undue delay, describing the breach in clear and plain language and including information on measures taken to mitigate adverse effects, unless exceptions apply (e.g., encryption was used) [1][3].

Under DORA, as a financial entity, the bank must report the major ICT-related incident (the ransomware attack) to the relevant competent authority using the prescribed templates after collecting and analyzing all relevant information. This initial notification must include all information necessary for the authority to assess the significance and possible cross-border impacts. The bank must also provide updates whenever the status of the incident changes significantly and a final report when root cause analysis and impact assessment are complete. The bank may outsource reporting obligations but remains fully responsible. The competent authority will share the information with other relevant EU bodies and authorities as appropriate [2].

regulation_query: AI system for credit scoring of consumers, high-risk AI system, obligations under AI Act, risk management, transparency, data governance, human oversight, documentation, conformity assessment
cited_chunk_ids: aia-en-article-16-0-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-9-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-9-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-9-3-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-9-4-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-9-5-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-9-6-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-9-7-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-9-8-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-9-9-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-9-10-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-53-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-53-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-53-3-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-53-4-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-53-5-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-53-6-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-53-7-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-55-1-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-55-2-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-55-3-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-50-3-2026-07-27 aia-en-article-25-4-2026-07-27
answer: The AI model used for credit scoring of consumers is likely considered a high-risk AI system under the AI Act. Therefore, the bank as a provider or deployer of such a high-risk AI system must comply with the obligations set out for high-risk AI systems. These include ensuring compliance with the requirements in Section 2 of the Regulation, having a quality management system in place, keeping technical documentation, maintaining logs, undergoing conformity assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, drawing up an EU declaration of conformity, affixing the CE marking, complying with registration obligations, taking corrective actions if needed, and demonstrating conformity upon request by national authorities [4]. Additionally, a risk management system must be established, implemented, documented, and maintained throughout the lifecycle of the high-risk AI system, including identification, evaluation, and mitigation of risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights, with special consideration for vulnerable groups such as persons under 18 [2]. If the AI model is a general-purpose AI model, additional obligations for providers of such models apply, including technical documentation, information provision to AI system providers, copyright compliance, and public summaries of training data [1]. If the model has systemic risk, further obligations such as adversarial testing, systemic risk assessment, incident reporting, and cybersecurity measures apply [3]. The bank must also ensure transparency obligations if the AI system involves biometric categorisation or emotion recognition, but this is not specified for credit scoring [5]. Finally, if the bank is a deployer rather than a provider, it must ensure compliance with these obligations and cooperate with providers as necessary [7].

regulation_query: Geltung der Datenschutz-Grundverordnung (DSGVO) bei gleichzeitiger Anwendbarkeit der KI-Verordnung (AI Act), Verhältnis der DSGVO zur KI-Verordnung, Datenschutzrechtliche Pflichten bei Einsatz von KI-Systemen

answer: Ja, die DSGVO gilt weiterhin für die Verarbeitung personenbezogener Daten im Zusammenhang mit den in der KI-Verordnung festgelegten Rechten und Pflichten. Die KI-Verordnung berührt die DSGVO nicht und lässt deren Anwendung unberührt, insbesondere in Bezug auf den Schutz personenbezogener Daten, der Privatsphäre und der Vertraulichkeit der Kommunikation [3](7).

regulation_query: DORA, ICT incident reporting obligations, 72-hour notification requirement, banks
cited_chunk_ids: dora-en-article-19-1-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-3-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-4-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-5-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-6-2022-12-27 dora-en-article-19-8-2022-12-27
answer: DORA Article 19 requires financial entities, including banks, to report major ICT-related incidents to the relevant competent authority within time limits to be laid down in accordance with Article 20, paragraph 1, point (a), point (ii). However, the exact time limit (such as 72 hours) is not specified in Article 19 itself but is to be determined by the delegated acts referred to in Article 20. Therefore, it is not explicitly stated in Article 19 that banks must report every ICT incident within 72 hours; the specific time limits are set elsewhere [1].
